query: Which experimental or audit designs (vignettes, behavioral tasks, mystery-reviewer audits) provide causal benchmarks for scale validity?

response.query: Which experimental or audit designs (vignettes, behavioral tasks, mystery-reviewer audits) provide causal benchmarks for scale validity?
response.answer: Regression discontinuity designs, instrumental variable designs, and propensity score matching provide causal benchmarks for scale validity. These designs help establish causal relationships when randomized experiments are not feasible.

The strongest quasi-experimental designs for causal inference are regression discontinuity designs, instrumental variable designs, matching and propensity score designs, and comparative interrupted time series designs. results.title: WORKSHOP: Causal Inferences for Experimental and Quasi-Experimental Designs
results.content:
ate CTSI

15 May 2025
Causal inference is central to the social, behavioral, and biomedical sciences. Although our research questions tend to be causal in nature, whether causal claims can be made depends on whether a list of assumptions are met regarding study design and statistical analyses. In this workshop, John Felt, PhD, will present approaches for designing experimental and quasi-experimental studies that facilitate causal inference from the perspective of three complimentary schools of thought: Potential Outcomes, Plausible Threats to Validity, and Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs). Hands-on experience with analytic approaches to facilitate causal inference will also be provided in R, a free and open-source statistical computing and graphics software. Users are encouraged to download and install R and R Studio prior to the workshop. A tutorial for downloading R and R Studio can be found here. Participants will leave this workshop with an introductory understanding of casual inference that they can start implementing in studies with new data collection as well as in secondary data analyses.

results.title: [PDF] Observational causal evaluations with quasi-experimental designs
results.content: Observational causal evaluations with quasi-experimental designs The goal of this document is to provide helpful resources for OES team members engaged in observational, usually retrospective, causal projects. Observational causal projects differ in important ways from the prospective randomized designs that make up the core of OES work. These studies rely on observational data – data in which the researchers have not themselves assigned the treatment or intervention – to identify causal relationships using a quasi-experimental design (QED). This design is a set of assumptions, evidence, and methods that may enable valid causal inferences from the observational data.

results.title: Ensuring Validity in Educational Experimental Designs • Teachers Institute
results.content: When conducting educational research, ensuring the validity of your experimental design is absolutely crucial. In this blog, we’ll explore how to ensure both internal and external validity in your experimental designs, as well as how to address potential sources of error that could compromise your study. * Understanding validity in experimental research. ## Understanding validity in experimental research. There are multiple types of validity, and for experimental research, two of the most important are internal validity and external validity. In other words, if you want to say that one thing caused another, internal validity ensures that the results of your study are truly due to the experimental manipulation, and not some other factor. To boost internal validity, researchers use various strategies to control for these potential threats. While internal validity is about establishing a clear cause-and-effect relationship in your experiment, external validity is concerned with whether your study’s findings can be generalized beyond the specific conditions of your study. For example, if you conduct an experiment on the effectiveness of a teaching method in a single classroom of college students, external validity asks whether your findings can be generalized to other classrooms, other schools, or even other countries. If your study lacks external validity, it means the conclusions may not be applicable to other situations, limiting the broader relevance of your research. To enhance external validity, researchers take steps to ensure that their findings are as generalizable as possible. * **Field experiments:** Conducting your research in a natural, real-world setting (rather than a controlled laboratory environment) increases ecological validity. One of the challenges in experimental research is balancing internal and external validity. On the other hand, improving external validity by conducting studies in natural settings might introduce confounding variables that threaten internal validity. By understanding the potential threats to validity and using appropriate strategies to control for them, researchers can design experiments that not only provide accurate causal relationships but also offer insights that are generalizable to real-world educational settings. **What strategies have you used to ensure the validity of your experimental designs?** Think about the types of threats you might face and how you can address them in your research planning.
